propositions.text: Whether retrospective changes to sentence conditions can constitute 'punishment' violating s. 11(h) of the Charter.
propositions.quote: This Court must decide whether retrospective changes to the conditions of a sentence may in some circumstances constitute “punishment” in violation of the s. 11 (h) right not to be punished twice for the same offence.

propositions.text: Distinction between sentence imposed and conditions of sentence in criminal law.
propositions.quote: The criminal law distinguishes between the sentence imposed on an offender and the conditions of the sentence.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains the issue of whether retrospective changes to sentence conditions violate s. 11(h) and distinguishes sentence from conditions.

propositions.text: APR was established in 1992 as a simplified parole process for first-time non-violent offenders.
propositions.quote: Established by legislation enacted in November 1992, APR was a simplified process that allowed first-time non-violent offenders to be considered for parole on the basis of a single question

paragraphs.summary: The Court states APR was created in 1992 as a simplified parole process for first-time non-violent offenders.

propositions.text: Canadian Criminal Justice Association criticized APR's violent recidivism test as unreliable.
propositions.quote: the Canadian Criminal Justice Association had expressed concerns about the violent recidivism test, noting that “[n]o system of predicting future behaviour can be safely based upon such a single factor.”

propositions.text: APR would allow offenders with violent records to qualify.
propositions.quote: It argued that APR would be available to some offenders who “have records with previous incarceration in Provincial institutions for offences including those of violence”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent reports criticism from the Canadian Criminal Justice Association about APR's test and eligibility.

propositions.text: APR was expanded in 1997 to include earlier eligibility for day parole.
propositions.quote: the APR process was expanded in 1997 to include earlier eligibility for day parole: after six months, or one sixth of the sentence, whichever was longer

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes APR was expanded in 1997 to allow earlier day parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Criticism of APR continued, recommending tightening eligibility and changing recidivism criteria.
propositions.quote: a parliamentary sub-committee... recommended “tightening the eligibility criteria” for APR... and “changing the risk of recidivism criterion to be taken into account by the National Parole Board”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent notes ongoing criticism recommending stricter APR eligibility and recidivism criteria.

propositions.text: Correctional Service Review Panel found statutory release and APR less effective than discretionary release.
propositions.quote: Correctional Service of Canada Review Panel concluded that “statutory release and accelerated parole have both undermined discretionary release and generally have not proved as effective as discretionary release in mitigating violent reoffending”

paragraphs.summary: The respondent cites a 2007 report criticizing APR's effectiveness compared to discretionary release.

propositions.text: Parliament repealed APR provisions retrospectively via AEPA in 2011, eliminating earlier release possibility.
propositions.quote: Parliament repealed the relevant provisions... the repeal applied retrospectively... Each of them would have been eligible for early day parole under the repealed provisions.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Parliament repealed APR retrospectively in 2011, affecting eligibility for early day parole.

propositions.text: Whether retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violates s. 11(h) right not to be punished twice.
propositions.quote: The question before this Court is whether the retrospective application of the delayed eligibility for day parole... violated the respondents’ right... not to be punished anew for their offences.

paragraphs.summary: The Court frames the issue of whether retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violates s. 11(h).

propositions.text: s. 11(h) applies and retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violated the right not to be punished again, unjustified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: I find that s. 11 (h) applies to the respondents’ claim. The retrospective application of delayed day parole eligibility violated the respondents’ s. 11 (h) right not to be “punished . . . again”, and that violation was not justified under s. 1 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes s. 11(h) applies and retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violated it unjustifiably.

propositions.text: No need to address s. 7 claim after finding s. 11(h) violation.
propositions.quote: I do not find it necessary to address the respondents’ claim with respect to the more general right guaranteed by s. 7 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The Court declines to address the s. 7 claim after finding a s. 11(h) violation.

propositions.text: Appeal from BC Court of Appeal upholding BC Supreme Court decision in respondents' favour.
propositions.quote: This is an appeal from a decision in which the British Columbia Court of Appeal upheld a summary trial decision of the British Columbia Supreme Court. Both courts found in the respondents’ favour.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes the appeal is from BC courts both ruling for respondents.

propositions.text: Respondents were first-time non-violent offenders eligible for APR at sentencing.
propositions.quote: The respondents... were all serving federal penitentiary sentences. As first-time, non-violent offenders, all three were eligible for APR under the system in place at the time of their sentencing

paragraphs.summary: The Court states respondents were first-time non-violent offenders eligible for APR at sentencing.

propositions.text: APR was automatic, paper-based, with a lower parole release test and no discretion to deny if test met.
propositions.quote: The APR application was automatic... The review was conducted on paper, without a hearing... the Board had no discretion to decide against releasing the offender

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes APR as automatic, paper-based, with a lower parole release test and no discretion to deny.

propositions.text: From 1997, APR day parole eligibility triggered earlier than normal parole.
propositions.quote: beginning in 1997, the APR process for day parole was triggered at an earlier date than in the normal process

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes APR day parole eligibility was earlier than normal parole from 1997.

propositions.text: AEPA repealed APR provisions and applied repeal retrospectively to offenders already serving sentences.
propositions.quote: Sections 3 and 5 of the AEPA repealed the CCRA ’s APR provisions... while s. 10(1) of the AEPA made the abolition of APR apply retrospectively to offenders already serving their sentences.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) states APR does not apply to offenders sentenced before or after repeal date.
propositions.quote: the accelerated parole review process set out in sections 125 to 126.1... does not apply, as of that day, to offenders who were sentenced... before, on or after the day of that coming into force.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains AEPA repealed APR provisions retrospectively, with s. 10(1) applying repeal to all offenders.

propositions.text: Repeal replaced earlier day parole eligibility with normal parole timing and changed review process and parole test.
propositions.quote: This changed the timing of eligibility for day parole... It also changed the review process... and the test for granting parole... reverted to the more onerous one of “undue risk to society”

paragraphs.summary: The Court details how repeal delayed day parole eligibility, changed review process, and raised parole test standard.

propositions.text: Repeal delayed day parole eligibility for respondents by 3, 9, and 21 months respectively.
propositions.quote: The immediate effect of the repeal was to delay the day parole eligibility dates of all three respondents: Mr. Whaling’s by three months, Ms. Slobbe’s by nine months, and Mr. Maidana’s by twenty-one months.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states repeal delayed respondents' day parole eligibility by varying months.

propositions.text: Respondents challenged constitutionality of s. 10(1) AEPA by summary trial in BC Supreme Court.
propositions.quote: The respondents challenged the constitutionality of s. 10(1) of the AEPA by way of a summary trial in the British Columbia Supreme Court.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes respondents challenged s. 10(1) AEPA constitutionality in BC Supreme Court summary trial.

propositions.text: Holmes J. found s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) as additional punishment, not justified under s. 1.
propositions.quote: Holmes J., the summary trial judge, held that s. 10(1) of the AEPA infringed s. 11 (h) of the Charter because it amounted to additional punishment, and that it was not saved under s. 1 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The BC Supreme Court judge found s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) and was not justified under s. 1.

propositions.text: Holmes J. reasoned s. 11(h) prevents additional punishment after conviction and sentence.
propositions.quote: [s.] 11(h)’s protections carry on past trial, conviction (or acquittal), and sentence, to prevent any additional trial or punishment for the offence with which the person was once charged

paragraphs.summary: The BC Supreme Court judge reasoned s. 11(h) prevents additional punishment after conviction and sentence.

propositions.text: Punishment occurs when a consequence is part of sanctions for an offence and furthers sentencing principles.
propositions.quote: As a general rule, it seems to me that the consequence will constitute a punishment when it forms part of the arsenal of sanctions to which an accused may be liable in respect of a particular offence and the sanction is one imposed in furtherance of the purpose and principles of sentencing.

propositions.text: Delayed parole eligibility is punishment in criminal sentencing context, supported by Supreme Court decisions.
propositions.quote: She pointed out that delayed parole eligibility is clearly used as “punishment” in the context of criminal sentencing, citing several decisions of this Court, including R. v. Shropshire, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 227, R. v. Chaisson, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 1118, and R. v. Zinck, 2003 SCC 6, [2003] 1 S.C.R. 41.

propositions.text: Parole ineligibility from sentence or retrospective CCRA amendment is not materially different due to overlapping objectives.
propositions.quote: parole ineligibility imposed as part of a sentence under the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46 , is not materially different from parole ineligibility resulting from the retrospective amendment of the CCRA , since the objectives and functions of the two processes can and do overlap.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found delayed parole eligibility is punishment, citing case law and that retrospective parole ineligibility is similar to sentencing parole ineligibility.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA has a punitive purpose and its retrospective alteration of day parole eligibility is punitive in effect.
propositions.quote: Holmes J. found that there was “abundant evidence” that its purposes were punitive in nature (para. 112). She also found that the effect of the retrospective alteration of day parole eligibility was punitive

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility alteration significantly affects how offenders serve sentences.
propositions.quote: this alteration would have a “significant actual effect on the way in which the two offenders who are still in prison will serve their sentences” (para. 113).

propositions.text: Changes to parole law that significantly limit parole eligibility of already sentenced offenders constitute additional punishment.
propositions.quote: “such changes do not include significant limitations, regardless of any exercise of the Board’s discretion, to the parole eligibility of offenders” who have already been sentenced (para. 114). A change that includes such limitations occasions additional punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s. 10(1) AEPA punitive in purpose and effect, significantly limiting parole eligibility and constituting additional punishment.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) AEPA infringes s. 11(h) of the Charter and is not saved under s. 1.
propositions.quote: Having established an infringement of s. 11 (h), Holmes J. found that the infringement was not saved under s. 1 of the Charter .

propositions.text: Objectives of retrospective repeal included maintaining public confidence in justice administration.
propositions.quote: the objectives underlying the retrospective application of the repeal, which included maintaining or restoring public confidence in the administration of justice, were pressing and substantial

propositions.text: Attorney General failed to show s. 10(1) impaired s. 11(h) rights no more than necessary.
propositions.quote: the Attorney General of Canada had not shown that the provision impaired the respondents’ s. 11 (h) rights no more than was necessary to attain Parliament’s objectives.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) declared invalid to extent it applies retrospectively to offenders sentenced before March 28, 2011, effective immediately.
propositions.quote: Holmes J. declared s. 10(1) to be invalid to the extent that it made the AEPA apply retrospectively to offenders sentenced before March 28, 2011, the date the AEPA came into force. The declaration was to have immediate effect.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) and was invalid retrospectively, not justified under s. 1 despite pressing objectives.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal upheld trial judge, finding s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy including sanctions after sentencing.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal upheld the trial judge’s decision, although with a few variations in reasoning. Levine J.A., writing for the court, found that the purpose of s. 11 (h) is to protect against double jeopardy, and that it applies to sanctions imposed after sentencing.

propositions.text: Retrospective legislative lengthening of jail time by delaying parole eligibility violates s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: She found that the retrospective legislative lengthening of the time the respondents would spend in jail that resulted from the delaying of their parole eligibility violated their right under s. 11 (h) not to be “punished again” (para. 71).

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found retrospective parole delay violated s. 11(h) as double jeopardy protection against punishment after sentencing.

propositions.text: Distinction between sentencing judge and Board roles does not change conclusion that s. 10(1) AEPA is punishment.
propositions.quote: Levine J.A. emphasized the distinction between the role of the sentencing judge and that of the Board under the CCRA , and mentioned that it is improper for a judge to take parole administration into consideration in the sentencing process. This did not alter her conclusion that s. 10(1) of the AEPA nonetheless amounted to punishment

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal noted sentencing and parole roles differ but still found s. 10(1) AEPA constituted punishment.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) aims to prevent being punished twice for the same offence after conviction.
propositions.quote: She stated that the purpose of s. 11 (h) is to ensure that a person cannot be punished a second time for an offence for which he or she has already been tried and convicted.

propositions.text: Issue is meaning of “punishment” under s. 11(h), focusing on whether consequence is part of sentencing sanctions and furthers sentencing principles.
propositions.quote: The issue was the meaning of “punishment” for the purposes of s. 11 (h), and this turned on whether the consequence in this case “forms part of the arsenal of [possible] sanctions” and furthers the “purpose and principles of sentencing”, as required by Rodgers (para. 63).

propositions.text: Effect of delayed parole eligibility by legislation is analogous to judge-imposed delayed parole, thus punishment violating s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: she held that the effect of the delayed parole eligibility imposed by way of legislation was analogous to that of delayed parole eligibility imposed by a judge, the latter of which is clearly punishment (citing Chaisson and Zinck). In its effect, therefore, s. 10(1) of the AEPA violated s. 11 (h) of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal held s. 11(h) prevents double punishment; delayed parole eligibility by legislation is punishment violating s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal agreed legislation was in response to pressing concern but insufficient evidence showed minimal impairment of rights under s. 1.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal also agreed with the trial judge’s finding that although the legislation was enacted in response to a pressing and substantial concern, the Attorney General had not provided sufficient evidence that it impaired the respondents’ rights as little as possible, which meant that it could not be saved under s. 1 of the Charter .

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal agreed s. 10(1) AEPA could not be justified under s. 1 due to insufficient evidence of minimal rights impairment.

propositions.text: Retrospective application of s. 10(1) AEPA violates s. 11(h) right not to be punished again.
propositions.quote: The respondents submit that the retrospective application provision, s. 10(1) of the AEPA , violates their right under s. 11 (h) of the Charter not to be “punished . . . again”.

propositions.text: Punishment should be broadly read beyond duplication of proceedings.
propositions.quote: They urge a broad reading of the term “punishment” that is not limited to the duplication of criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings.

propositions.text: Retrospective repeal eliminating early day parole eligibility is punitive in effect and purpose.
propositions.quote: the retrospective application of the repeal, which eliminated the eligibility for early day parole of offenders who had already been sentenced, was punitive in its effect. The respondents also argue, parting ways with the Court of Appeal on this point, that it was punitive in its purpose.

paragraphs.summary: The respondents argue s. 10(1) AEPA's retrospective repeal violates s. 11(h) with punitive effect and purpose, urging broad punishment definition.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) should be narrowly read to exclude elimination of early day parole eligibility as punishment.
propositions.quote: The Crown urges a narrow, textual reading of s. 11 (h) that would exclude the elimination of early day parole eligibility from the definition of “punishment”.

propositions.text: Retrospective repeal aims for rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety, not punishment; effect reflects this.
propositions.quote: It argues that the retrospective application of the repeal was adopted in furtherance of the goals of rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety and confidence in the administration of justice, not that of punishment. The effect of that application reflects this non-punitive purpose.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) requires duplication of criminal proceedings to be engaged.
propositions.quote: In this Court, the Crown further argues that s. 11 (h) is not engaged, because being “punished . . . again” requires a duplication of proceedings that are criminal in nature in respect of the same matter.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues s. 11(h) requires duplication of criminal proceedings and that repeal aims at non-punitive goals, excluding punishment.

propositions.text: Whether s. 11(h) applies absent duplication of proceedings and scope of punishment concept under s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: I will begin with this last question of whether s. 11 (h) applies absent a duplication of proceedings. I will then consider the scope of the “punishment” concept in the context of s. 11 (h) before inquiring into whether the impugned provision constitutes “punishment” in its purpose or in its effect.

paragraphs.summary: The Court will first consider if s. 11(h) applies without duplicated proceedings, then the punishment scope, then if the provision is punishment.

propositions.text: Trial court and Court of Appeal did not address whether s. 11(h) applies without duplication of proceedings.
propositions.quote: Neither the trial court nor the Court of Appeal dealt with this question.

propositions.text: Both courts agreed s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, focusing on meaning of punishment.
propositions.quote: The two courts agreed that s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, which Levine J.A. defined as protection “from being tried or punished again for an offence for which the offender has already been found guilty and punished” (para. 45), and they focused their analyses on the meaning of “punishment” for the purposes of s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes lower courts did not address s. 11(h) application without duplicated proceedings but agreed it protects against double jeopardy.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) states right not to be tried or punished again if finally found guilty and punished.
propositions.quote: Section 11 (h) of the Charter reads as follows: 11. Any person charged with an offence has the right . . . (h) if finally acquitted of the offence, not to be tried for it again and, if finally found guilty and punished for the offence, not to be tried or punished for it again;

paragraphs.summary: The Court quotes s. 11(h) stating the right not to be tried or punished again after final conviction and punishment.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted s. 11(h) to protect against double jeopardy, mirroring ICCPR art. 14.7.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s purpose in enacting s. 11 (h) was to protect against double jeopardy. Section 11 (h) mirrors the language and purpose of art. 14.7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 999 U.N.T.S. 171, which reads: 7. No one shall be liable to be tried or punished again for an offence for which he has already been finally convicted or acquitted in accordance with the law and penal procedure of each country.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states s. 11(h) was enacted to protect against double jeopardy, mirroring ICCPR article 14.7.

propositions.text: Double jeopardy law is complex and includes protection against multiple trials and multiple punishments.
propositions.quote: Under existing Canadian law there is certainly no one rule on double jeopardy. The subject is one of the utmost complexity and subtlety and is certainly in need of clarification. The law provides protection against harassment of multiple trials for the same act but also protection against multiple punishment.

paragraphs.summary: Academic commentary states double jeopardy law is complex, protecting against multiple trials and punishments.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) has narrow scope and little impact on double jeopardy and double punishment protection.
propositions.quote: As several authors have noted, the scope of s. 11 (h) is narrow (see M. L. Friedland, “Legal Rights Under The Charter ” (1982), 24 Crim. L.Q. 430, at pp. 435 and 449; Stuart, at p. 467). Stuart states that s. 11 (h) has had “little impact on the protection of the accused against double jeopardy and double punishment”, in part because of this narrow scope (ibid.).

propositions.text: Broader double jeopardy interpretations may fit better under s. 7 of the Charter.
propositions.quote: Both Friedland and Stuart suggest that broader interpretations of double jeopardy may fit more easily into s. 7 of the Charter (Friedland, at p. 435; Stuart, at p. 468).

propositions.text: Sections 11(g) and 11(i) explicitly address retrospectivity and harsher punishment after crime commission.
propositions.quote: there are two provisions that deal explicitly with retrospectivity: s. 11 (g), which protects against retroactive criminal legislation, and s. 11 (i), which protects against the imposition of a harsher punishment where the punishment for the offence has been varied between the time of commission of the crime and the time of sentencing.

paragraphs.summary: Academic sources note s. 11(h) is narrow, broader double jeopardy fits s.7, and other sections address retrospectivity.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) applies to protect against being punished again even without a separate proceeding.
propositions.quote: In my view, it is not necessary to resort to a different Charter provision. The language of s. 11 (h), the academic literature and this Court’s jurisprudence support a reading of s. 11 (h) according to which the right not to be “punished . . . again” applies where an offender has been sentenced, even if no separate proceeding has taken place.

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes s. 11(h) protects against being punished again even absent a separate proceeding.

propositions.text: Plain meaning of s. 11(h) shows protection against being tried or punished again is independent and either suffices to engage s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: The disjunctive language of the words “tried or punished” clearly indicates that s. 11 (h)’s protection against additional punishment is independent of its protection against being tried again.

propositions.text: Conjunctive language “found guilty and punished” emphasizes disjunctive “tried or punished”.
propositions.quote: The conjunctive language of the words “found guilty and punished” further accentuates the disjunctive language of “tried or punished”.

propositions.text: Protection applies to harassment of multiple trials and additional punishment.
propositions.quote: as Stuart notes in respect of double jeopardy more generally, the protection applies to both the harassment of multiple trials and the harassment of additional punishment (p. 464).

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 11(h) language protects against being tried or punished again independently, covering multiple trials and punishments.

propositions.text: It is more questionable to punish without a proceeding than with one; s. 11(h) protects against punishment without trial.
propositions.quote: It would be far more questionable to punish someone without a proceeding than to punish him or her with a proceeding. The purpose of s. 11 (h) cannot be to protect against punishment imposed following a trial in which due process has been observed, but not against punishment imposed without the protections afforded by a trial.

paragraphs.summary: The Court reasons s. 11(h) must protect against punishment without trial, as that is more questionable than punishment after trial.

propositions.text: Narrow scope of s. 11(h) does not preclude protection against double punishment without new proceeding.
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, this does not preclude the application of s. 11 (h) to protect against double punishment where no new proceeding has taken place

propositions.text: s. 11(h) distinct from autrefois acquit and Kienapple rule against multiple convictions for same act.
propositions.quote: it is distinct from statutory and common law protections such as autrefois acquit, or the rule in Kienapple v. The Queen, [1975] 1 S.C.R. 729, against multiple convictions for separate offences based on a single act (R. v. Van Rassel, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 225, at p. 233).

propositions.text: Some authors focus on what constitutes a second proceeding for s. 11(h), but this does not limit s. 11(h) application to double punishment without proceeding.
propositions.quote: While some authors focus on the fine points of what constitutes a second proceeding for the purposes of s. 11 (h) (see P. W. Hogg, Constitutional Law of Canada (5th ed. Supp.), vol. 2, at p. 51-35), this does not limit the application of s. 11 (h) in cases of double punishment in which no such proceeding took place.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states s. 11(h) narrow scope does not exclude protection against double punishment without new proceeding, distinct from other doctrines.

propositions.text: Early s. 11(h) cases addressed double jeopardy from criminal charges after non-criminal sanctions, not punishment without second proceeding.
propositions.quote: The early cases with respect to s. 11 (h) concerned situations in which criminal charges were laid against an accused who had previously been sanctioned or disciplined in a non-criminal proceeding for the same act; the question was whether the non-criminal proceeding or sanction triggered the protection against double jeopardy (R. v. Wigglesworth, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 541, and R. v. Shubley, [1990] 1 S.C.R. 3). Those cases did not directly address the possibility of punishment without a second proceeding.

propositions.text: Crown cites McLachlin J. in Shubley that s. 11(h) protects against duplication in criminal proceedings, not two different proceedings from same act.
propositions.quote: The Crown cites the following comment made by McLachlin J. (as she then was) in Shubley (p. 19): “Section 11 (h) provides protection against duplication in proceedings of a criminal nature. It does not preclude two different proceedings, one criminal and the other not criminal, flowing from the same act” (A.F., at para. 59).

propositions.text: McLachlin J.'s comment must be read in context of inquiry into whether proceeding was criminal in nature.
propositions.quote: However, this passage must be read in context, as part of the Court’s inquiry into whether the proceeding in question was criminal “in nature”.

propositions.text: Protection against double jeopardy can be triggered by criminal proceedings or true penal consequences.
propositions.quote: Even in the early s. 11 (h) cases, it was found that the protection against double jeopardy could be triggered by proceedings that are criminal in nature or by “true penal consequences”.

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes early s. 11(h) cases addressed double jeopardy from criminal and non-criminal proceedings, and protection applies to criminal or penal consequences.

propositions.text: Rodgers case held s. 11 applies only when a person is charged with an offence, and DNA order application does not engage s. 11
propositions.quote: the protection extended by s. 11 can only be invoked when “[a] person [is] charged with an offence”. Therefore, in and of itself, the application for a DNA order does not at all engage s. 11

propositions.text: s. 11 applies to original criminal proceedings but question is if DNA order is further punishment
propositions.quote: there is no doubt that s. 11 applies to those criminal proceedings and the question then becomes whether the imposition of a s. 487.055 order constitutes further “punishment” for those offences

propositions.text: Court rejected Crown's narrow construction of s. 11(h) limiting it to duplication of criminal proceedings
propositions.quote: In Rodgers, the Court rejected the narrow construction of s. 11 (h) advanced by the Crown in the case at bar according to which it is limited to cases involving a duplication of proceedings that are criminal in nature

propositions.text: s. 11(h) protects against double punishment even without a second proceeding
propositions.quote: I find that s. 11 (h) does protect an offender who has been tried and sentenced against double punishment even in the absence of a second proceeding

propositions.text: Academic commentary on this issue is sparse and may need updating
propositions.quote: As to the paucity of academic commentary on this issue, it may be time to update the textbooks

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Rodgers supports that s. 11(h) protects against double punishment even without a second proceeding, rejecting Crown's narrow view.

propositions.text: Having concluded s. 11(h) allows double punishment claims without second proceeding, must determine if current case amounts to punishment
propositions.quote: Having concluded that s. 11 (h) does not preclude claims of double punishment where a second proceeding has not taken place, I must now determine whether the situation in the instant case amounts to punishment

paragraphs.summary: The Court concludes s. 11(h) allows double punishment claims without second proceeding and must decide if this case is punishment.

propositions.text: Scope of punishment under s. 11(h) has expanded over time with new cases
propositions.quote: The scope of “punishment” in the context of s. 11 (h) has expanded over the years as new cases have pushed the limits of old definitions

propositions.text: Criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings trigger s. 11(h) protection against double jeopardy
propositions.quote: It has always been clear that criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings trigger the protection against double jeopardy

propositions.text: Second criminal or quasi-criminal charge for same act engages s. 11(h) even if consequence is slight
propositions.quote: Thus, a second criminal or quasi-criminal charge with respect to the same act engages s. 11 (h) even if the consequence is slight

paragraphs.summary: The Court states s. 11(h) protection applies to criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings, including second charges for same act.

propositions.text: Wigglesworth held s. 11(h) may be triggered by non-criminal proceedings with true penal consequences
propositions.quote: Wigglesworth made it clear that the protection against double jeopardy may be triggered not only by proceedings that are criminal or quasi-criminal in nature, but also by non-criminal proceedings that result in a sanction with true penal consequences

propositions.text: True penal consequences include imprisonment or fines imposed to redress societal wrongs, not internal discipline
propositions.quote: a true penal consequence which would attract the application of s. 11 is imprisonment or a fine which by its magnitude would appear to be imposed for the purpose of redressing the wrong done to society at large rather than to the maintenance of internal discipline within the limited sphere of activity

paragraphs.summary: Wigglesworth held s. 11(h) applies to non-criminal proceedings with true penal consequences like imprisonment or fines.

propositions.text: Wigglesworth found internal disciplinary proceeding with possible imprisonment involved true penal consequences
propositions.quote: although the internal disciplinary proceeding against an RCMP officer was neither criminal nor quasi-criminal “in nature”, it was found to involve “true penal consequences” because the possible sanctions included imprisonment for up to one year

propositions.text: Shubley found internal prison disciplinary sanctions without fines or imprisonment did not meet true penal consequences
propositions.quote: a sanction imposed in an internal prison disciplinary proceeding — close confinement for a period of five days on a special diet — fell short of “true penal consequences”, in part because the possible sanctions involved neither fines nor imprisonment

paragraphs.summary: Wigglesworth found true penal consequences in disciplinary proceedings with imprisonment; Shubley found no true penal consequences without fines or imprisonment.

propositions.text: Rodgers revisited punishment definition, considering if DNA sample order constituted double punishment
propositions.quote: In Rodgers, the Court took the opportunity to revisit the definition of “punishment” it had articulated in Wigglesworth and Shubley

propositions.text: Charron J. accepted imprisonment and heavy fines as true penal consequences but said punishment not limited to these
propositions.quote: Charron J. accepted that imprisonment and heavy fines constitute “true penal consequences”, but reasoned that “punishment” is not limited to these two types of sanctions

propositions.text: Charron J. identified features of punitive sanctions including forfeiture, firearm prohibition, driving prohibition, restitution
propositions.quote: She mentioned various orders a sentencing court might make, such as an order for forfeiture, a firearm prohibition, a driving prohibition or an order for restitution

paragraphs.summary: Rodgers revisited punishment definition, with Charron J. expanding beyond imprisonment and fines to other punitive sanctions.

propositions.text: Rodgers two-part test: punishment if sanction is part of arsenal of sanctions and furthers sentencing purpose
propositions.quote: As a general rule, it seems to me that the consequence will constitute a punishment when it forms part of the arsenal of sanctions to which an accused may be liable in respect of a particular offence and the sanction is one imposed in furtherance of the purpose and principles of sentencing

propositions.text: Charron J. found DNA order not part of arsenal of criminal sanctions and not stigma attaching
propositions.quote: Charron J. found that a DNA order is no more a part of the arsenal of criminal sanctions than the taking of a photograph or fingerprints

propositions.text: Not all deterrent measures are punishment; example given of random traffic stops
propositions.quote: while it may have a deterrent effect, not all deterrent measures can be characterized as punishment

paragraphs.summary: Rodgers test defines punishment as sanction in arsenal of sanctions and furthers sentencing; DNA order not punishment as no stigma or criminal sanction.

propositions.text: Current case pushes limits of punishment concept, requiring revisiting s. 11(h) principles
propositions.quote: the case at bar once again pushes the limits of the “punishment” concept, requiring us to revisit the principles that define the scope of s. 11 (h)

propositions.text: Wigglesworth and Rodgers tests do not fully address current case question
propositions.quote: the question in the instant case eludes both tests

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds this case pushes punishment limits and Wigglesworth and Rodgers tests do not fully apply.

propositions.text: Issue is whether retrospective changes to parole eligibility constitute punishment
propositions.quote: this case requires us to determine whether retrospective changes to parole eligibility, which modify the manner in which an existing sanction is carried out, constitute punishment

propositions.text: Alleged punishment is frustration of offender's expectations about original sanction, not a second proceeding or discrete sanction
propositions.quote: The alleged punishment is neither a second proceeding nor a “sanction” in the sense contemplated in Rodgers. Rather, the offender’s expectations about the original punishment or sanction have been frustrated and this is said to constitute new punishment

paragraphs.summary: The Court identifies the issue as whether retrospective parole changes frustrating offender's expectations constitute punishment.

propositions.text: Rodgers test's first branch defines punishment by traditional Criminal Code sanctions, not parole changes
propositions.quote: In the first branch of the Rodgers test, “punishment” is defined by referring to the traditional forms of punishment provided for in the Criminal Code

propositions.text: Parole grant changes conditions of sentence, not reduction of sentence itself
propositions.quote: a grant of parole represents a change in the conditions under which a judicial sentence must be served, rather than a reduction of the judicial sentence itself

propositions.text: Changes to parole system generally not part of arsenal of sanctions in Rodgers test
propositions.quote: changes to the parole system do not generally form part of the “arsenal of sanctions” contemplated in Rodgers

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Rodgers test excludes parole changes as they alter sentence conditions, not sentence itself.

propositions.text: Incarceration is most severe deprivation of liberty and benchmark punishment under Criminal Code
propositions.quote: Incarceration is “the most severe deprivation of liberty known to our law”

propositions.text: Retrospective parole changes may extend incarceration, which is core punishment under Rodgers test
propositions.quote: a retrospective change to parole eligibility may have the effect of extending an offender’s term of incarceration

propositions.text: Incarceration and heavy fines are benchmark sanctions for assessing other sanctions under Rodgers test
propositions.quote: Incarceration and heavy fines are the benchmark sanctions against which other, less severe sanctions are assessed under the Rodgers test

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes incarceration is core punishment and retrospective parole changes may extend incarceration, engaging s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Rodgers test is overly formalistic for parole changes, excluding many but including marginal incarceration increases
propositions.quote: when applied in this context, the Rodgers test is overly formalistic, as the “arsenal of sanctions” test would exclude most changes to parole eligibility, whereas even marginal increases in the likelihood of additional incarceration easily meet the test

propositions.text: Rodgers test does not identify functional increases in punishment harshness from retrospective parole changes
propositions.quote: Rodgers test does not assist in identifying situations in which, from a functional rather than a formalistic perspective, the harshness of punishment has been increased

propositions.text: Rodgers test designed for discrete sanctions, not modifications of original sanction
propositions.quote: The Rodgers test was designed for a different purpose, namely to determine whether a discrete sanction — one that does not modify the original sanction — has the characteristics of a criminal sanction, and thus constitutes “punishment”

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds Rodgers test too formalistic and unsuitable for assessing retrospective parole changes as punishment.

propositions.text: Second branch of Rodgers test (furthers sentencing purpose) awkward for parole changes
propositions.quote: The second branch of the Rodgers test — whether the sanction furthers the purpose and principles of sentencing — is also an awkward fit in this situation

propositions.text: Parole principles like rehabilitation also apply in sentencing, so all retrospective parole changes could be said to further sentencing purpose
propositions.quote: rehabilitation and reintegration are principles applied in parole administration, but they are also sentencing principles

propositions.text: Not all retrospective parole changes are punitive despite furthering sentencing principles
propositions.quote: it is clear to me that not all such changes would be punitive

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds the second branch of Rodgers test awkward for parole changes, as not all such changes are punitive.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) precludes: (a) criminal/quasi-criminal proceedings again; (b) additional sanctions meeting Rodgers test; (c) retrospective changes adding punishment
propositions.quote: s. 11(h) precludes the following further state actions in relation to the same offence: (a) a proceeding that is criminal or quasi-criminal in nature; (b) an additional sanction or consequence that meets the two-part Rodgers test; and (c) retrospective changes to the conditions of the original sanction which have the effect of adding to the offender’s punishment

propositions.text: This case concerns retrospective repeal of APR provisions altering parole expectations, not repeal itself
propositions.quote: It is not the repeal of the APR provisions that is alleged to be unconstitutional, but the retrospective application of that repeal, which altered the parole expectations of offenders who had already been sentenced

paragraphs.summary: The Court identifies three types of double punishment under s. 11(h), with this case concerning retrospective parole changes adding punishment.

propositions.text: Charter s. 11(g) protects against retroactive criminal laws; s. 11(i) protects against increased punishment after crime commission
propositions.quote: s. 11 (g), which protects against retroactive criminal laws... s. 11 (i)... protects against increases in punishment between the time of commission of the crime and the time of sentencing

propositions.text: Peter Hogg states Canadian constitutional law lacks prohibition of retroactive laws except s. 11(g)
propositions.quote: [a]part from s. 11 (g), Canadian constitutional law contains no prohibition of retroactive (or ex post facto) laws

propositions.text: s. 11(g) and (i) express society's repudiation of retroactive punishment broadly defined
propositions.quote: Both these provisions express society’s repudiation of retroactive punishment, broadly defined

paragraphs.summary: The Court notes Charter s. 11(g) and (i) protect against retroactive criminal laws and increased punishment, reflecting repudiation of retroactive punishment.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, not expressly retroactivity
propositions.quote: Section 11(h) is not expressly concerned with retroactivity. Its purpose is to protect against double jeopardy

propositions.text: Early s. 11(h) cases involved offences existing at time of acts, no retroactive punishment issue
propositions.quote: the issue in the early cases on s. 11(h) was whether a person who had already been sanctioned in a non-criminal proceeding could subsequently be charged for the same act under the Criminal Code

propositions.text: s. 11(h) may be engaged without duplication of proceedings by retrospective parole modifications increasing punishment
propositions.quote: s. 11 (h) may be engaged where no duplication of proceedings has occurred. Retrospective modification of the parole system after an offender was sentenced may have the effect of increasing the offender’s punishment

propositions.text: Non-punitive legislative change can acquire punitive character if applied retrospectively
propositions.quote: A legislative change that is not in itself punitive can acquire a punitive character by being applied retrospectively

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, and retrospective parole changes can increase punishment engaging s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Offenders have constitutionally protected expectations as to sentence duration, not conditions
propositions.quote: Generally speaking, offenders have constitutionally protected expectations as to the duration, but not the conditions, of their sentences

propositions.text: Not all changes in parole management are punitive despite affecting liberty interest
propositions.quote: Various changes in the management of an offender’s parole are not punitive, even though they may engage the offender’s liberty interest

propositions.text: Cunningham held Charter s. 7 protects only significant changes amounting to further deprivation of liberty
propositions.quote: qualification must be significant enough to warrant constitutional protection... there must be a “substantial change in conditions amounting to a further deprivation of liberty”

paragraphs.summary: Cunningham held offenders have protected expectations on sentence duration, not conditions; only substantial changes depriving liberty warrant Charter protection.

propositions.text: Substantial change requirement from s. 7 context not imported into s. 11(h) context
propositions.quote: The requirement of a “substantial change in conditions amounting to a further deprivation of liberty” was articulated in the context of s. 7 , and I will not import it into that of s. 11(h)

propositions.text: Retrospective parole changes engaging s. 7 liberty interest may not constitute punishment under s. 11(h)
propositions.quote: Retrospective changes to the parole system that engage a liberty interest under s. 7 will not necessarily constitute punishment for the purposes of s. 11(h)

propositions.text: Offender has expectation of liberty based on parole system at sentencing; thwarting it may engage liberty interest
propositions.quote: the Court recognized that an offender has an expectation of liberty that is based on the parole system in place at the time of his or her sentencing, and that thwarting that expectation may engage a constitutionally protected liberty interest

propositions.text: Cunningham: more liberty on mandatory supervision than in prison
propositions.quote: One has ‘more’ liberty, or a better quality of liberty, when one is serving time on mandatory supervision than when one is serving time in prison

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds s. 7 substantial change test not imported to s. 11(h); offender's liberty expectation based on parole system may be constitutionally protected.

propositions.text: Not all parole liberty expectations are constitutionally protected; line drawing needed
propositions.quote: not all expectations of liberty in the parole context are constitutionally protected... Some line drawing becomes necessary

propositions.text: Some retrospective parole changes amount to new punishment under s. 11(h), others do not
propositions.quote: Some retrospective changes to the parole system affect the expectation of liberty... to such an extent that they amount to new punishment, while other changes have a more limited impact and do not trigger Charter protection

paragraphs.summary: The Court finds some retrospective parole changes amount to new punishment under s. 11(h), others do not; line drawing is necessary.

propositions.text: No universal formula for retrospective parole changes; context-specific analysis required
propositions.quote: I will not articulate a formula that would apply to every case, because such a formula is not needed to resolve this appeal and the effect of every retrospective change will be context-specific

propositions.text: Dominant consideration is extent to which offender's settled liberty expectation is thwarted by retrospective legislative action
propositions.quote: the dominant consideration in each case will in my view be the extent to which an offender’s settled expectation of liberty has been thwarted by retrospective legislative action

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility changes that automatically lengthen incarceration constitute additional punishment contrary to s. 11(h)
propositions.quote: a retrospective change to the rules governing parole eligibility that has the effect of automatically lengthening the offender’s period of incarceration constitutes additional punishment contrary to s. 11 (h) of the Charter

propositions.text: Such categorical thwarting of liberty expectation is clearest case of retrospective double punishment under s. 11(h)
propositions.quote: A change that so categorically thwarts the expectation of liberty of an offender who has already been sentenced qualifies as one of the clearest of cases of a retrospective change that constitutes double punishment in the context of s. 11 (h)

paragraphs.summary: The Court holds no universal formula exists; key is thwarting of liberty expectation; automatic incarceration lengthening is clear double punishment under s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Sentencing judges may consider delayed parole eligibility as part of the sentence in certain circumstances under the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: the punitive effect of delayed parole eligibility is expressly recognized in the Criminal Code , which empowers a sentencing judge to consider delayed parole eligibility to be part of the sentence in certain circumstances.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges should not consider parole eligibility in assessing sentence fitness (Zinck, para. 18).
propositions.quote: a sentencing judge is not to consider parole eligibility in assessing the fitness of the sentence (Zinck, at para. 18)

propositions.text: Section 743.6(1) allows courts to impose delayed parole eligibility for denunciation or deterrence.
propositions.quote: s. 743.6(1) empowers a court to impose delayed parole eligibility for the purpose of denunciation or of specific or general deterrence.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges may increase parole ineligibility for second degree murder (Chaisson, para. 12).
propositions.quote: a sentencing judge may increase the parole ineligibility period of an offender convicted of second degree murder (Chaisson, at para. 12)

propositions.text: Sentencing courts determine fixed parole ineligibility terms in murder cases (R. v. Wust, para. 24).
propositions.quote: In murder cases, the sentencing court will determine a fixed term of parole ineligibility: s. 745.4 of the Code.

propositions.text: Parole ineligibility duration is the only punishment difference between first and second degree murder (Shropshire, para. 23).
propositions.quote: the duration of parole ineligibility is the only difference in terms of punishment between first and second degree murder, which “clearly indicates that parole ineligibility is part of the ‘punishment’

paragraphs.summary: The court finds sentencing judges may impose delayed parole eligibility as part of punishment, citing Criminal Code and case law.

propositions.text: Retrospective delayed parole eligibility imposed by legislation constitutes punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.
propositions.quote: retrospectively imposing delayed parole eligibility on offenders who have already been sentenced constitutes punishment. Where Parliament imposes through retrospective legislation a consequence that sentencing judges may themselves impose for the purpose of punishment, the s. 11 (h) protection against double punishment applies.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes retrospective delayed parole eligibility imposed by legislation is punishment protected against by s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Whether retrospective parole changes constitute double punishment depends on circumstances and risk of additional incarceration.
propositions.quote: Whether less drastic retrospective changes to parole constitute double punishment will depend on the circumstances of the particular case.

propositions.text: Retrospective changes not substantially increasing incarceration risk are generally not punitive.
propositions.quote: Generally speaking, a retrospective change to the conditions of a sentence will not be considered punitive if it does not substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration.

propositions.text: Individualized decision-making and procedural rights reduce risk of additional incarceration.
propositions.quote: Indicators of a lower risk of additional incarceration include a process in which individualized decision making focused on the offender’s circumstances continues to prevail and procedural rights continue to be guaranteed in the determination of parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Replacing automatic release with discretionary release was constitutional in Cunningham due to procedural safeguards.
propositions.quote: the replacement of an automatic release system with a discretionary release system was found to be constitutional in Cunningham owing in part to various procedural safeguards, including a hearing and the entitlement to counsel.

propositions.text: Presence of procedural safeguards is relevant to likelihood of increased punishment severity under s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: the presence or absence of such safeguards is relevant in considering the likelihood of the punishment’s severity being increased.

propositions.text: A change extending incarceration without regard to individual circumstances and procedural safeguards violates s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: A change that directly results in an extension of the period of incarceration without regard to the offender’s individual circumstances and without procedural safeguards in the assessment process will clearly violate s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains when retrospective parole changes violate s. 11(h), focusing on increased incarceration risk and procedural safeguards.

propositions.text: A law may violate the Charter in purpose or effect; failing purpose test ends inquiry (Big M Drug Mart).
propositions.quote: A law may violate the Charter in its purpose or in its effect: “If the legislation fails the purpose test, there is no need to consider further its effects, since it has already been demonstrated to be invalid” (R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, at p. 334).

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal considered purpose then effect of s. 10(1) AEPA; trial judge found violation in both; Court of Appeal found violation in effect only.
propositions.quote: both the trial judge and the Court of Appeal considered the purpose of the law first, followed by its effect. The trial judge held that s. 10(1) of the AEPA violates the Charter in both its purpose and its effect, whereas the Court of Appeal declined, because the effect of s. 10(1) renders it unconstitutional, to rule on the constitutionality of its purpose.

propositions.text: The court agrees with Court of Appeal that s. 10(1) violates Charter in its effect, for different reasons.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Court of Appeal, but for different reasons, that s. 10(1) violates the Charter in its effect.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees s. 10(1) AEPA violates the Charter in effect, noting prior courts' analyses of purpose and effect.

propositions.text: Overall purpose of AEPA is not disputed and is constitutionally valid.
propositions.quote: First of all, the overall purpose of the AEPA is not at issue. I agree with the Court of Appeal, which found that there is no serious dispute about the validity of that purpose

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found no serious dispute about AEPA's purpose validity, supported by evidence of parole regime goals.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General points to evidence it provided at trial that supports repealing APR to enhance the purposes and principles of parole regimes... These purposes are entirely within the constitutional powers of the government, and the respondents take no issue with the AEPA on that basis.

propositions.text: The issue is Parliament's decision to apply repeal retrospectively to already sentenced offenders.
propositions.quote: What is at issue is Parliament’s decision to make the repeal apply retrospectively, by means of s. 10(1) of the AEPA , to offenders who had already been sentenced.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds AEPA's overall purpose valid but focuses on the issue of its retrospective application to sentenced offenders.

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility changes violate s. 11(h) if their purpose is to prolong incarceration.
propositions.quote: where legislation makes retrospective changes to parole eligibility, it will violate s. 11 (h) if its purpose is to prolong the offender’s period of incarceration.

propositions.text: Crown says retrospective repeal furthers rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety, and confidence goals by applying immediately and uniformly.
propositions.quote: The Crown submits that Parliament’s decision to have the repeal apply retrospectively was made in furtherance of the goals of rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety and confidence in the administration of justice. These goals were better served by having the repeal apply “immediately and uniformly to all offenders, including those already sentenced but not yet released” (A.F., at para. 84).

propositions.text: Respondents and trial judge argue retrospective application aims at denunciation, deterrence, and punishment.
propositions.quote: The respondents contend, and the trial judge so held, that this argument conceals the true purpose of the retrospective application provision. Both they and Holmes J. have cited Hansard to show that retrospective application was meant to serve the purposes of denunciation, deterrence and punishment.

propositions.text: Central question: Did Parliament intend to lengthen incarceration time for already sentenced offenders?
propositions.quote: These arguments circle around the central question: Was Parliament’s purpose to lengthen the time to be served in jail by offenders who had already been sentenced?

paragraphs.summary: The court states retrospective parole changes violate s. 11(h) if intended to prolong incarceration; parties dispute Parliament's purpose.

propositions.text: MP's statement suggests Parliament intended to extend incarceration for offenders already sentenced.
propositions.quote: one Member of Parliament had said that if the repeal was not retroactive, the victims of a notorious crime committed before the repeal “will never have any kind of justice served”

propositions.text: This suggests the retrospective provision's purpose was incompatible with s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: This strongly suggests that Parliament intended to extend the period of incarceration of offenders who had already been sentenced, which would mean that the purpose of the provision was incompatible with s. 11 (h).

paragraphs.summary: An MP's statement suggests Parliament intended to extend incarceration, implying incompatibility with s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Court accepts Crown's articulation of Parliament's purpose as applying legitimate parole objectives universally.
propositions.quote: I accept the Crown’s articulation of Parliament’s purpose for the following reasons... I see nothing prima facie unconstitutional about the purpose of applying legitimate parole objectives universally to all offenders.

propositions.text: Parole administration is distinct from sentencing; Parliament returned to pre-APR parole rules for all offenders.
propositions.quote: Parole administration is distinct from sentencing. Parliament, responding to criticism of APR, saw fit to adopt a different approach by returning to the normal pre-APR parole rules, and considered it desirable to pursue the objectives underlying those rules in respect of all offenders, including those who had already been sentenced.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts Crown's view that Parliament's purpose was legitimate parole objectives applied universally, distinct from sentencing.

propositions.text: Parliament's authority to modify sentence conditions is limited when modification constitutes punishment.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s authority to modify the conditions of an existing sentence... is limited where the effect of a modification is such that it constitutes punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Parliament's power to modify sentence conditions is limited if the modification constitutes punishment.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) AEPA deprived respondents of early day parole consideration, lengthening minimum incarceration.
propositions.quote: The effect of the retrospective application provision, s. 10(1) of the AEPA , was to deprive the three respondents of the possibility of being considered for early day parole, which was an expectation they had had at the time they were sentenced.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 10(1) AEPA deprived respondents of early day parole consideration, extending incarceration.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) punished respondents again by retrospectively delaying day parole eligibility automatically without regard to individual circumstances.
propositions.quote: In my view, s. 10(1) had the effect of punishing the respondents again. It retrospectively imposed a delay in day parole eligibility... The effect — extended incarceration — was automatic and without regard to individual circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 10(1) punished respondents anew by automatically delaying day parole eligibility without individual consideration.

propositions.text: Delayed parole eligibility imposed by retrospective legislation is analogous to judicially imposed delayed parole eligibility and constitutes punishment under s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: The imposition of a delay in parole eligibility in this case is analogous to the imposition of delayed parole eligibility by a judge under the Criminal Code as part of the sentence... Imposing this same consequence by means of retrospective legislation triggers the protection against double punishment set out in s. 11 (h).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds retrospective delayed parole eligibility is punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.

propositions.text: Formal distinction between parole administration and sentencing does not shield retrospective parole ineligibility extension from s. 11(h) scrutiny.
propositions.quote: This formal distinction does not change the basic point that... the new period of parole ineligibility thwarted the expectations of liberty... Nor does the fact that the legislation... was passed in the context of the CCRA rather than that of the Criminal Code shield Parliament’s measure from the scrutiny under s. 11 (h) of the Charter that would otherwise apply.

propositions.text: Parliament cannot avoid s. 11(h) scrutiny by choosing to amend CCRA instead of Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: If that were the case, Parliament could enact punitive laws resulting in double punishment simply by choosing to amend the CCRA rather than the Criminal Code .

paragraphs.summary: The court holds that the distinction between parole administration and sentencing does not exempt retrospective parole changes from s. 11(h) scrutiny.

propositions.text: Constitutionality of other APR abolition aspects was not seriously argued; retrospective changes require detailed analysis.
propositions.quote: the constitutionality of other aspects of the abolition of APR was not seriously argued... every retrospective change must be analyzed in detail before conclusions can be drawn as to its possible punitive effect.

propositions.text: Greater impact on offender's liberty expectation or likelihood of additional incarceration increases chance of s. 11(h) violation.
propositions.quote: The greater the impact on the offender’s settled expectation of liberty, or the greater the likelihood of additional incarceration, the more likely it is that a given retrospective change will violate s. 11 (h).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes other APR abolition aspects were not argued; retrospective changes must be analyzed for punitive effect under s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Respondents argue s. 10(1) violates s. 7 by depriving liberty against fundamental justice principles.
propositions.quote: The respondents argue, in the alternative, that s. 10(1) violates s. 7 of the Charter by depriving the offender of liberty in contravention of the principles of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Fundamental justice requires accused be tried and punished under law in force at offence time (R. v. Gamble).
propositions.quote: It is fundamental to any legal system... that an accused must be tried and punished under the law in force at the time the offence is committed.

propositions.text: Having found s. 10(1) offends s. 11(h), court finds it unnecessary to decide on s. 7 application.
propositions.quote: Having already found that the impugned provision offends s. 11 (h) of the Charter , I find it unnecessary to decide on the application of s. 7 .

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue s. 10(1) violates s. 7; court finds s. 11(h) violation sufficient and declines to decide s. 7 issue.

propositions.text: Court prefers addressing specific Charter guarantees over s. 7 when both pleaded (R. v. Harrer, Généreux, Pearson).
propositions.quote: When both s. 7 and a specific guarantee under the Charter are pleaded, this Court has generally shown a preference for dealing with the specific guarantee...

propositions.text: Legal rights under ss. 8-14 are specific instances of fairness under s. 7; s. 7 may sometimes offer broader protection.
propositions.quote: this Court decided that ss. 8 to 14 of the Charter , the “legal rights”, are specific instances of the basic tenets of fairness... which are now entrenched as a constitutional minimum standard by s. 7 .

propositions.text: Section 11(h) specifically protects against retrospective delayed parole eligibility punishment; court declines to address s. 7 arguments.
propositions.quote: Section 11 (h) protects against the specific infringement alleged in the case at bar: the retrospective legislative imposition of delayed parole eligibility, which has the effect of punishing the offender anew. I therefore decline to address the arguments with respect to s. 7 .

paragraphs.summary: The court explains preference for specific Charter guarantees and declines to address s. 7 as s. 11(h) covers the issue.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal found s. 10(1) AEPA objectives pressing and substantial but failed minimal impairment.
propositions.quote: The trial judge held, and the Court of Appeal agreed, that the objectives of s. 10(1) of the AEPA are pressing and substantial, but they both found that the provision failed at the minimal impairment stage.

propositions.text: The court agrees with the result that s. 10(1) fails minimal impairment.
propositions.quote: I agree with this result.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with prior courts that s. 10(1) AEPA's objectives are pressing but it fails minimal impairment.

propositions.text: Parliament had evidence that APR was ineffective and could legislate to improve the system.
propositions.quote: Parliament based its decision to abolish APR on considerable evidence... that the system was not working effectively.

propositions.text: Trial judge found ensuring sentences as administered reflect court sentences is pressing and substantial objective.
propositions.quote: The trial judge found that the objective of ensuring that sentences as administered are consistent with the sentences courts impose... is pressing and substantial (para. 121).

propositions.text: Parliament's decision to apply objectives to all offenders reflects legitimate concern for uniformity and confidence in justice system.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s decision to apply these same objectives to all offenders... reflects its legitimate concern to ensure uniformity of parole administration and maintain confidence in the justice system.

propositions.text: Legislative measure including retrospective application is rationally connected to objectives.
propositions.quote: Having agreed that these objectives are pressing and substantial, I also find that the legislative measure... is rationally connected to the objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament had pressing objectives and the AEPA's retrospective application is rationally connected to them.

propositions.text: Crown failed to prove no less intrusive alternative to retrospective application existed.
propositions.quote: the Crown has failed to provide compelling evidence that that uniformity would be impaired if the APR system continued to apply to offenders who were sentenced under it.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal concluded sentence management objectives do not justify depriving respondents of constitutional rights.
propositions.quote: Sentence management objectives in general... do not rise to such significance that justifies implementing them in a manner that deprives the respondents of their constitutional rights.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees Crown failed to prove no less intrusive alternative to retrospective application; prior court found objectives don't justify rights deprivation.

propositions.text: Prospective repeal was available alternative to achieve objectives without violating s. 11(h) rights.
propositions.quote: In my view, having the repeal apply only prospectively was an alternative means available to Parliament that would have enabled it to attain the objectives... without violating the s. 11 (h) rights of offenders who had already been sentenced.

propositions.text: Enacting Charter-infringing legislation damages confidence in justice system; no evidence prospective repeal would undermine objectives.
propositions.quote: the enactment of Charter -infringing legislation does great damage to that confidence. The Crown has produced no evidence to show why the alternative of a prospective repeal... would have significantly undermined its objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds prospective repeal was a viable alternative that would not violate rights and that Charter-infringing laws damage confidence.

propositions.text: The remedy was overly broad because s. 10(1) was declared invalid entirely, but only delay in day parole eligibility infringed rights.
propositions.quote: The Crown argues in this Court that the remedy ordered by the summary trial judge and subsequently upheld by the Court of Appeal was overly broad, because she declared s. 10(1) to be invalid in its entirety, whereas only the delay in day parole eligibility — one consequence of the retroactive application of the repeal — had been found to infringe the respondents’ rights.

propositions.text: Offenders should benefit only from early day parole eligibility, not all abolished APR system aspects.
propositions.quote: The Crown submits that the offenders should benefit not from all aspects of the abolished APR system, including automatic referral to the Board, a review conducted on paper and more favourable release criteria, but only from the one aspect — early day parole eligibility — whose elimination has been found to be unconstitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the remedy was too broad, invalidating all of s. 10(1) though only delay in day parole eligibility infringed rights, and offenders should benefit only from early day parole eligibility.

propositions.text: Both courts held retrospective elimination of early day parole eligibility unconstitutional.
propositions.quote: Both of the courts below held that the retrospective application of the elimination of early day parole eligibility was unconstitutional.

propositions.text: No serious analysis was done on constitutionality of eliminating other APR aspects retrospectively.
propositions.quote: No serious analysis was conducted into the constitutionality of the retrospective application of the elimination of other aspects of the APR system.

propositions.text: Punishment identified was delayed day parole eligibility, not changes to review procedure or release criteria.
propositions.quote: The “punishment” identified by the summary trial judge and upheld by the Court of Appeal was the delayed date for day parole eligibility, not the changes to the review procedure or to the criteria for release.

paragraphs.summary: The courts below found only the retrospective elimination of early day parole eligibility unconstitutional, not other APR changes.

propositions.text: Retrospective modification of review procedure and release criteria resembles sentence management changes accepted in Cunningham.
propositions.quote: Although I will not decide this issue, the retrospective modification of the review procedure and the release criteria would seem to me to resemble the change relating to sentence management that this Court accepted in Cunningham.

propositions.text: Changes in how a sentence is served are not contrary to fundamental justice principles.
propositions.quote: A change in the form in which a sentence is served, whether it be favourable or unfavourable to the prisoner, is not, in itself, contrary to any principle of fundamental justice.

propositions.text: Legislative imposition of delayed day parole eligibility prolongs incarceration and constitutes punishment under s. 11(h).
propositions.quote: In the instant case, I have held that the legislative imposition of delayed day parole eligibility, by effectively prolonging the minimum period of incarceration of offenders who had already been sentenced, constitutes “punishment” for the purposes of s. 11 (h).

propositions.text: No other AEPA aspects found unconstitutional; pre-APR parole procedures can apply with early day parole timelines.
propositions.quote: I have not found other aspects of the AEPA to be unconstitutional. At first blush, I do not see anything impractical or offensive about having the pre-APR parole procedures that are now in force apply while at the same time following the timelines for early day parole eligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds changes to review procedure resemble accepted sentence management changes; delayed day parole eligibility is punishment; other AEPA aspects are constitutional.

propositions.text: Courts below did not receive submissions on limited declaration now proposed; caution is needed before changing remedy.
propositions.quote: However, the courts below did not receive submissions on the limited declaration now being proposed in this Court. This Court must exercise caution in deciding whether to depart from the remedy crafted by the trial judge and upheld by the Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: Cautious approach favours upholding full declaration of invalidity for two reasons.
propositions.quote: In my view, this cautious approach favours upholding the full declaration of invalidity. I draw this conclusion for two reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no prior submissions on limited remedy and favors upholding full invalidity declaration cautiously for two reasons.

propositions.text: Early day parole was adopted as part of APR; cannot presume Parliament would enact it alone.
propositions.quote: First, early day parole eligibility was adopted as a component of APR, and I cannot presume that Parliament would have enacted the legislation establishing it in the absence of the rest of the APR system.

propositions.text: Severance test asks if valid part is so bound to invalid part it cannot survive independently (Schachter).
propositions.quote: The test for severance is whether the constitutionally sound portion of the scheme is so inextricably bound up with the part declared invalid that what remains cannot independently survive (Schachter v. Canada, [1992] 2 S.C.R. 679, at p. 697).

propositions.text: Doubts about respondents' claim that early day parole is functionally bound to APR; no evidence to decide.
propositions.quote: I harbour doubts about the respondents’ submission that early day parole was functionally bound up with the rest of the APR scheme. However, to conclude that it was not in the absence of evidence on how early day parole would work in combination with normal parole procedures would be to overstep my judicial role.

propositions.text: Cannot presume Parliament would enact early day parole legislation on its own.
propositions.quote: I cannot presume that Parliament would have enacted the legislation establishing early day parole on its own.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds early day parole was part of APR and cannot presume Parliament would enact it alone; severance test requires evidence.

propositions.text: Even if early day parole could stand alone, severance is not workable here due to legislative dependencies.
propositions.quote: Second, even if it were clear that early day parole eligibility could stand, functionally, on its own, severance would not be workable in the context of this legislation.

propositions.text: Section 119.1 depends on ss. 125 and 126 defining eligibility and release terms.
propositions.quote: Section 119.1 , which established the earlier eligibility period for day parole, was expressly dependent on both s. 125 , which defined the class of offenders who were automatically eligible for accelerated parole review, and s. 126, which set out the procedural and substantive terms for release on parole.

propositions.text: Section 119.1 sets eligibility period for offenders eligible under ss. 125 and 126.
propositions.quote: 119.1 The portion of the sentence of an offender who is eligible for accelerated parole review under sections 125 and 126 that must be served before the offender may be released on day parole is six months, or one sixth of the sentence, whichever is longer.

propositions.text: Section 126.1 specifies ss. 125 and 126 apply to early day parole under s. 119.1.
propositions.quote: Section 126.1 specified that ss. 125 and 126 applied to the early day parole option established by s. 119.1 .

paragraphs.summary: The court finds severance unworkable because s. 119.1 depends on ss. 125 and 126, which define eligibility and release terms for early day parole.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA repealed ss. 125, 126, 126.1 retrospectively, withdrawing early day parole rights.
propositions.quote: Section 10(1) of the AEPA made the repeal of ss. 125 , 126 and 126.1 of the CCRA apply retrospectively and thus, in effect, withdrew the right to be considered for early day parole from offenders who had been eligible for such consideration prior to the enactment of the repeal provisions.

propositions.text: Section 119.1 cannot operate without ss. 125, 126, and 126.1 and is meaningless without them.
propositions.quote: The specific reference in s. 119.1 to “the sentence of an offender who is eligible for accelerated parole review under sections 125 and 126 ” means that this section cannot operate without ss. 125 , 126 and 126.1 and is thus meaningless without them.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 10(1) repealed ss. 125-126.1 retrospectively, withdrawing early day parole rights, and s. 119.1 is meaningless without those sections.

propositions.text: Reading s. 10(1) to repeal ss. 125-126.1 retrospectively but not s. 119.1 is impossible to implement.
propositions.quote: To read s. 10(1) of the AEPA down to make the repeal of ss. 125 to 126.1 apply retrospectively but not that of s. 119.1 , as the Crown proposes, would result in a provision that would be impossible to implement.

propositions.text: Therefore, uphold declaration of invalidity of all of s. 10(1).
propositions.quote: I would therefore uphold the declaration of invalidity of all of s. 10(1) .

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes that partial reading of s. 10(1) is impossible and upholds invalidity of all of s. 10(1).

propositions.text: Dismiss appeal and uphold trial judge's remedy.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss the appeal and uphold the remedy ordered by the trial judge.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) of AEPA violates s. 11(h) of the Charter and is of no force or effect.
propositions.quote: Section 10(1) of the AEPA violates s. 11 (h) of the Charter and is accordingly of no force or effect.

propositions.text: Sections 125, 126, 126.1 and 119.1 of CCRA continue to apply to offenders sentenced before AEPA's coming into force.
propositions.quote: Sections 125 , 126 , 126.1 and, by implication, 119.1 of the CCRA therefore continue to apply to offenders who were sentenced prior to the coming into force on March 28, 2011, of the AEPA .

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed.
propositions.quote: Appeal dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, finds s. 10(1) violates s. 11(h), and upholds continued application of ss. 125-126.1 and 119.1 to pre-AEPA offenders.
